Boasters
bōst'ərz
n. pl. (vaunters; men who make an empty show of what they are or have)
From Middle English bosten, to brag. The Greek alazon named the wandering quack who claimed cures he could not perform — a pretender whose word outruns his substance.

Biblical Definition

Boasters appear in both of the great catalogues of a society under judgment. Romans lists them among the marks of men given over: “Backbiters, haters of God, despiteful, proud, boasters, inventors of evil things, disobedient to parents” (Rom 1:30). Second Timothy places them at the head of the perilous times: “For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy” (2Ti 3:2). In both lists the boaster stands next to the proud, and the order is instructive: pride is the root in the heart, boasting is the fruit in the mouth. James names the sin and passes sentence in a sentence: “But now ye rejoice in your boastings: all such rejoicing is evil” (Jas 4:16). He is not condemning cheerfulness but the particular gladness a man takes in his own arrangements for tomorrow, as though the breath in his lungs were his own possession. The Psalmist sees the same tongue and asks God to deal with it: “The LORD shall cut off all flattering lips, and the tongue that speaketh proud things” (Psa 12:3). Scripture leaves one boast standing — the man who glories in the LORD — and destroys every other.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a boaster as one who boasts, glories, or vaunts ostentatiously; to boast is to vaunt, to brag, to display one's own worth or actions in high terms.

expand to see more

BOAST, v.i. To brag, or vaunt one's self; to make an ostentatious display, in speech, of one's own worth, property, or actions.

2. To glory; to speak with laudable pride and exultation of meritorious persons or things.

BOASTER, n. One who boasts, glories or vaunts ostentatiously.

Covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers. 2 Tim. iii.

Key Scripture

Rom 1:30 — "Backbiters, haters of God, despiteful, proud, boasters, inventors of evil things, disobedient to parents,"

2Ti 3:2 — "For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy,"

Jas 4:16 — "But now ye rejoice in your boastings: all such rejoicing is evil."

Psa 12:3 — "The LORD shall cut off all flattering lips, and the tongue that speaketh proud things:"

Modern Corruption

Boasting has been rehabilitated as confidence and self-advertisement made a duty of the working life, while James calls the rejoicing itself evil.

expand to see more

The alazon of the Greek was a figure of contempt: the travelling pretender whose claims could not be cashed. Our own age has made his manner a discipline. A man is taught to present himself, to build a name, to speak of his work in terms that outrun it, and to call the whole performance confidence; the boaster is no longer the man everyone laughs at but the man everyone is advised to imitate. Scripture does not answer this with false modesty, which is only pride wearing a plainer coat. It answers with a question that removes the ground of boasting altogether: what hast thou that thou didst not receive? If a man's gift, health, wit and opportunity were all given, then boasting is not an overstatement of his merit but a misattribution of God's. That is why Paul can allow one glorying and no other, and why the boasts of Romans 1 stand in a list of men who did not like to retain God in their knowledge.

James is dealing with a boast so ordinary that it hardly sounds like one: to day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain. There is no bragging in it, only planning — and the apostle calls the rejoicing evil. What offends is not the plan but the assumed possession of the time in which to execute it, when the man does not know what shall be on the morrow and his life is a vapour. The correction he gives is not to stop planning but to plan under God: if the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that. That little clause, said honestly, is the death of boasting in a Christian's speech, because it acknowledges every hour as a loan. The corruption to name here is the reverse habit, common in professing circles, of announcing what God is going to do through a man as though the announcement secured it. Boasting about the future in religious language is still boasting about the future.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek alazon (G213), a vaunting pretender; alazoneia (G212), the boasting itself; set against kauchaomai (G2744) rightly directed — glorying in the LORD.

expand to see more

Greek alazon (G213) — a boaster, a braggart whose claim exceeds his substance; Romans 1:30, 2 Timothy 3:2.

Greek alazoneia (G212) — boasting, vainglory; the pride of life that is not of the Father; James 4:16, 1 John 2:16.

Greek kauchaomai (G2744) — to glory, to boast; forbidden of self and commanded of the Lord; 1 Corinthians 1:31, Galatians 6:14.

Greek huperephanos (G5244) — proud, showing oneself above others; the companion word in both catalogues; Romans 1:30, James 4:6.

Hebrew halal (H1984) — to shine, to praise, and in the reflexive to boast; let not the wise man glory in his wisdom; Jeremiah 9:23-24.

Usage

"“Covetous, boasters, proud” — the mouth's fruit standing next to the heart's root."

"“All such rejoicing is evil” — the ordinary boast of a year's plans."

"“The tongue that speaketh proud things” — what the LORD will cut off."
